prize_parts.citation: For the dynamical mean-field theory of strongly correlated electron systems, from the infinite-dimension limit to the quantum-impurity mapping that explains the Mott transition and correlated metals.

statement.case_for: Dynamical mean-field theory is the first controllable, non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons. Vollhardt's infinite-dimension limit and the Georges-Kotliar mapping onto a self-consistent quantum impurity problem gave a clear and general account of the Mott transition and of correlated metals, which earlier approaches could not. It is a conceptual discovery with more than three decades of independent use. Through DFT+DMFT it also became a standard route to realistic correlated materials, and cold-atom Hubbard simulators and spectroscopy have tested it. Three names cover the decisive conceptual steps. After the opening ballots I still hold that this is the strongest case on originality, durability and breadth. I do not claim it has the broadest support, because it does not.
statement.case_against: The main weakness is attribution. Metzner's part in the infinite-dimension limit and the contributions of Müller-Hartmann, Jarrell and Rozenberg fall outside any three-name prize, and I cannot call that gap trivial. Single-site DMFT is also quantitatively unreliable where nonlocal correlations dominate, as in low-dimensional and cuprate-like physics. Only I put this candidate first, and nobody else's top four includes it, so I must accept that it has not persuaded the committee. The strongest competing case is B029, which draws support from six members and has a cleaner two-name attribution and a more precisely bounded achievement.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first because Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's 1e-18 realisation are cleanly credited, independently reproduced, and relevant to the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that B029 is the best-bounded and best-attributed candidate on the list, and the confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, PTB and SYRTE is the kind of maturity I look for. I ranked it fifth, but I now see that as too low. My remaining reservation is about kind rather than quality. Much of the lattice clock's recognition rests on precision metrology that follows from the frequency-comb and ion-control prizes of 2005 and 2012. I do not think that decides the case, and I would support B029 as a prize if the committee prefers it. I still think DMFT introduces a more fundamental new idea.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and the twisted bilayer graphene configuration second. She regards the clock as a transparent atomic-physics result with large impact and calls two laureates a natural, uncontroversial configuration.
responses.response: I accept the point about the clean two-name configuration, and it is a real advantage over my own candidate. I would qualify the claim of low controversy. Lindroth herself lists Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and Hinkley as contributors, and the 1e-18 result depends on many clock groups. That is less serious than the Metzner problem in B035, but it is not nothing. On B031 I agree with her ranking, since the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction preceded the measurement. I disagree that this makes it ready now, because the origin of the correlated states is still debated.

responses.point: Johansson puts trapped-ion quantum computing first, with Cirac, Zoller and Blatt. The Cirac-Zoller proposal and Blatt's gates make a coherent trio and a foundation for quantum information hardware.
responses.response: I take the scientific weight of the proposal seriously, and the three names are well matched. I ranked it outside my top eight because a large part of the achievement, ion control and quantum-state engineering, overlaps the 2012 prize. I also think the computational payoff is still unfolding, and Johansson himself raises overlap with 2012 and the open race among qubit platforms. I would want the committee to say precisely what is new beyond Wineland and Haroche before it commits. Calling the work a foundation does not settle that.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery first. The experimental discovery has never been honoured, and credit should go to those who conceived and led ATLAS and CMS, namely Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee.
responses.response: The importance of the discovery is beyond doubt, and I accept that it is overdue. My difficulty is attribution. Two collaborations of several thousand people made the discovery, and a prize to three project leaders honours construction and leadership more than a discovery in the physics sense. The committee would be on firmer ground if it could point to a decisive individual contribution. I would not block it, but I would need that attribution argument made explicitly. I also note that B012 has only four rankings in the opening, so support for it is narrower than its first-place votes suggest.

uncertainties: Whether Metzner's omission from the credited names is acceptable, or whether it disqualifies B035 as drafted.
How much of the lattice-clock achievement is already covered by the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the pairing mechanism and the correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene are settled enough to make B031 mature.
The committee may weigh breadth of opening support above my judgement of conceptual depth, and I have no independent way to settle that.
statement.conflict_note: My own research uses DFT, DFT+DMFT and electronic-structure methods, so I am a user and a potential beneficiary of B035. B031 is also close to my field of electronic-structure theory. I am the former Chair for the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which is relevant to the B004 overlap discussion. My profile does not state a personal or institutional link to any credited candidate, so no specific recusal conflict is apparent. The committee may still want to record that DMFT-based methods are part of my own work.
